text: Given an array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements, in any order. Try to beat n log n time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Order among the k doesn't matter, and the answer is unique — so there's no ambiguity at the k-th frequency boundary? And k is at most the number of distinct elements?

Okay. Counting frequencies is unavoidable. The interesting part is picking the top k. Key observation: a frequency can be at most n, so it's a small integer — I can bucket by frequency and skip comparison sorting entirely.

Let me weigh the options. Sorting by frequency is n log n. A size-k min-heap is n log k — good. But this problem reminds me of bucket sort, and it fits because frequencies are bounded by n. If bucket f holds the values with frequency f, the whole thing is linear — the index itself is the sorted frequency, so I just scan from high to low.

Here's the plan. One: count each value in a hash map. Two: put each value into the bucket for its frequency. Three: scan the buckets from n down and collect values until I have k. Two things worth flagging. First, the bucket array is size n plus one, because the max frequency is n when all elements are equal. Second, I scan high to low and stop the moment I have k — the index encodes the ordering, so no sort or heap is needed. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. Three blocks: count into a hash map, push each value into the bucket at its frequency, then walk the buckets from n downward, collecting into result. That matches the plan. One detail worth flagging — the outer condition, result size below k, plus the inner break, both stop as soon as I have k. The break only leaves the current bucket; the outer check is what stops the next one from opening. So I never touch the low-frequency buckets.

Let's dry-run the code. One, one, one, two, two, three, with k equal to two and n equal to six. The counts are three ones, two twos, one three. Value one, with frequency three, sits in the highest bucket, so it's taken first. The row that matters is i equals two: value two completes k equals two, and bucket one is never scanned. Answer: one and two. Corner cases: four sevens with k equal to one uses bucket four — frequency equals n, which is why the size is n plus one. And k equal to the number of distinct elements returns them all. All check out.

Time is linear — count, bucket, and scan are all linear, and the buckets hold at most n values total. Space is linear for the counts map and the bucket array. That beats the n log n target. One more thing — if this were a stream, or distinct values were sparse relative to n, I'd prefer a size-k min-heap, at n log k time with only k items in the heap. Buckets need the frequency bound up front.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: spotting that frequency is bounded by n so bucket sort applies, the size n plus one detail for the all-equal case, and knowing when a heap is the better tradeoff. Good work.
